lines.trans: Paco Cerdeña is my ex, a very important Spanish film producer.
We were married for five years.
Imagine the contacts I have in the film world.
They've had dinner at my house and stayed over to sleep.
Give me a name and I'll tell you a story.
You're a bit tense, aren't you?
A shot to loosen you up. Come on, relax.
Do you want a shot, Lidia?
I'll pass. I don't drink, Paquita.
You do drink.
I don't drink.
Since I'm drinking, we all drink.
At least toast. Come on, smile.
Gorgeous, all of you. I love it.

meanings.note: Marks many specific human direct objects without a separate English word; in poco a poco it belongs to the expression little by little.
Keep ñ: ano is a different word.

examples.trans: I've been here for two years.
This year I am working a lot.
Since I'm drinking, we all drink.
We toast the bride and groom.
We're having dinner at my house.

examples.text: Las casas del pueblo son blancas.

examples.trans: We were married for five years.
They've had dinner at my house.

meanings.note: Proper name from the episode.

examples.text: Es la boda de Paco Cerdeña.

examples.trans: We're going to the cinema tonight.

meanings.note: Introduces a role or a comparison. No written accent in this use; the question word cómo is different.

examples.text: No hace falta que lo diga.
examples.trans: There is no need for me to say it.

meanings.note: Mandatory contraction of de + el before a masculine singular noun.

examples.text: Vamos a la boda del productor.
examples.trans: We're going to the producer's wedding.

examples.text: Es una estrella del cine español.
examples.trans: She's a star of Spanish cinema.
You're a bit tense, aren't you?

meanings.note: The choice after experto is en; English may use at, in or on according to the following activity or subject.

examples.trans: She is an expert on film.

meanings.note: A state or location.
In estar bien or estar mal, evaluates an action or situation.
Invariable in the plural: el/la ex, los/las ex.

examples.trans: You look gorgeous in the photo.

meanings.note: Auxiliary before a past participle; does not express possession.
The impersonal present is hay, not ha.
In farewell expressions, introduces the next meeting; do not translate the farewell word for word.
Proper name from the episode.

examples.trans: Do you want a shot, Lidia?

meanings.note: Unstressed first-person singular object; its exact direct/indirect/reflexive role depends on the verb.
Todo el mundo means everyone and takes a singular verb.

examples.trans: I want to see the world.

meanings.note: A standalone answer can precede a separate negative statement, producing two occurrences of no.
Proper name from the episode.

examples.text: Vamos a la boda de Paco.

meanings.note: Source-attested name or surname. Name history is supplied separately with its own evidence and uncertainty; no unverified full name is inferred.

examples.text: Todo el mundo quiere a Paquita.

examples.trans: It's difficult, but I can do it.
I want to go, but I am working.

meanings.note: In poco a poco, the two occurrences belong to one expression meaning gradually.

examples.trans: Little by little, I'm understanding it.

meanings.note: Links a clause after a judgment in the first lesson example; introduces a relative clause about people in the second.

examples.trans: I'm looking for people who work here.

examples.text: El vestido queda un poco grande.
examples.trans: The dress is a little big.

examples.text: Tú te quedas en la oficina.

meanings.note: A desire for a thing or an action.
Affection for a person, as in the lesson.

examples.trans: I'll send it to him now.

meanings.note: Identity, profession or a characteristic; compare estar for a state or location.

examples.trans: A shot to loosen you up.
Come on, smile for the photo.

examples.text: Te llamo la semana que viene.

meanings.note: Possession, relationships and many fixed expressions.
Tener algo claro means to understand it or have a firm view of it.

examples.text: Tiene muy claro lo que quiere.
examples.trans: She is very clear about what she wants.
You're a bit tense, aren't you?

meanings.note: Before a noun it is a determiner; standing alone, todos/todas can mean everyone or all of them.

examples.trans: Come on, let's go to the car.

meanings.note: Subject pronoun; often omitted when the verb already identifies the person.
